item.title: Conditional Indexing Lower Bounds and Normalization Boundaries for Elastic Subsequence Matching
item.description: arXiv:2610.12938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study static indexes for exact subsequence matching over all equal-length windows of a time series. Under deterministic SETH, for every fixed $\beta\ge1$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, we exclude $O(N^\beta)$ preprocessing together with $O(N^{1-\delta})$ worst-case query time on domains containing the reduction's polylogarithmic query lengths. The bounded-error counterpart assumes randomized SETH. The results cover specified warping, bottleneck, edit, subsequence, local-alignment, and complexity-adjusted scores. Their reductions share a data-independent query interface but require different arguments for all-window soundness. We give complete representative proofs for the distinct mechanisms and state the changes needed by related scores. For soft-DTW, integer scaling yields an exact Boolean-predicate reduction in Word-RAM; a model with exact transcendental primitives requires a separate assumption. For independent window-wise Z-normalization, balanced coordinate gadgets and shifted-window moment bounds yield exact lower bounds for squared-cost DTW and discrete Fr\'echet distance. We give finite-word comparisons and a specified length-dependent rounding rule preserving these gaps. Raw and normalized discrete Fr\'echet constructions also exclude feasible-solution approximation within any fixed factor below two. Finally, we prove conditional signal-attenuation bounds for normalized anchor constructions and a fast index under the all-window common-mean promise.
item.dc:creator: Zemin Chao, Zitong Li, Xiangyu Gao, Hongzhi Wang

item.title: Subset Sum and Integer Programming Feasibility Test in Near-Optimal Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.12953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given an integer $t$ and a set of integers in $[N]$, Subset Sum asks whether there exists a subset that sums to $t$. A long open problem is whether Subset Sum can be solved in $O(N)$ time. We show that Subset Sum can be solved in $O(N^{1 + \varepsilon})$ time where $\varepsilon > 0$ is an arbitrarily small constant. Our result also generalizes to multi-sets in multi-dimension. That is, for any fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon >0$, the $d$-dimensional subset sum can be solved in $O(n + N^{d + \varepsilon})$ time. As an application, for any fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon$, feasibility test of integer programming with $d$ constraints can be done in $O(N^{d+\varepsilon} \mathrm{poly}(\ell_{\mathrm{in}}))$ time, where $N$ is the maximum absolute value in the constraint matrix and $\ell_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the input size. Although the algorithm is quite involved, its high-level idea is clear. It is already known that when the input set is dense and $t$ lies in the interior of the zonotope, then Subset Sum is easy to solve [Galil-Margalit '91, Bringmann-Wellnitz '21, Chen-Hu-Mao-Zhang '26]. Our key observation is that a sparse input can exhibit a dense structure when lifted to higher dimension. We show that such a lifting can be done efficiently. After lifting, the interior of the zonotope is easy to tackle, and one only needs to deal with the thin area near the boundary of the zonotope. Then we show that the boundary area can be decomposed into subproblems and solved recursively, and that there cannot be too many recursion levels since each level of recursive reduces the volume of the area significantly.
item.dc:creator: Lin Chen, Yuchen Mao, Guochuan Zhang

item.title: Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies
item.description: arXiv:2610.12991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases. We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020] Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents). These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.
item.dc:creator: Nick Arnosti, Rad Niazadeh, Pranav Nuti, Felipe Simon

item.title: Minimizing fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.13010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model minimization is a fundamental problem in formal methods, as smaller models can substantially reduce the complexity of model analysis and reasoning while preserving relevant semantic properties. This work studies the minimization of finite fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices while preserving global or local assertions in fuzzy modal logics, which are either fuzzy propositional dynamic logic or a restriction thereof, optionally enriched with nominals, converse modalities, and/or the universal program constructor. We prove that, whenever the multiplication operator of the underlying residuated lattice is right-continuous, the quotient model induced by the greatest fuzzy auto-bisimulation is a minimal reduction preserving global assertions. If the underlying fuzzy modal logic includes the universal program constructor, this quotient model is also a minimal reduction preserving local assertions and a minimal fuzzy Kripke model bisimilar to the original model. In the case where the universal program constructor is absent and the multiplication operator is additionally strictly monotone with respect to~1, we present the first algorithm for constructing a minimal reduction preserving local assertions; the resulting model is also a minimal bisimilar model.
item.dc:creator: Linh Anh Nguyen

item.title: Polynomial directed treewidth forces a large bramble with congestion two
item.description: arXiv:2610.13270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Brambles of constant congestion in directed graphs have interesting structural and algorithmic applications, and it is desirable to find the smallest function $f_c(k)$ such that if a digraph has directed treewidth at least $f_c(k)$, then it contains a bramble of size at least $k$ and congestion at most $c$. By the Directed Grid Theorem of Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC 2015], such a function $f_c(k)$ exists for every value $c \geq 2$ of the congestion. However, even using the recent improvements due to Hatzel et al. [FOCS 2024], the resulting function is a power tower of height $22$. Recently, Masa\v{r}\'ik et al. [SIAM J. Discrete Math. 2022] proved that, for congestion $8$, the function $f_8(k)$ can be made polynomial; more precisely, they showed that $f_8(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{48} \cdot \log^{13} k)$. They asked whether it is possible to decrease the congestion, ideally to $2$, even at the cost of a higher polynomial function. In this work we answer their question affirmatively with the best possible value of the congestion, by proving that $f_2(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{96}\cdot \log^{23} k)$. We also obtain smaller polynomials for higher congestion, namely $f_4(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{72} \cdot \log^{21} k)$ and $f_6(k) = \mathcal{O}(k^{66} \cdot \log^{18} k)$. Our results are inspired by the proof for congestion $8$, which we improve by introducing walkages. Walkages allow us to avoid technicalities of the original proof by translating ideas due to Reed and Wood [Eur. J. Comb. 2012] that work for undirected graphs to the directed setting. Our proofs are constructive and naturally yield polynomial-time algorithms to find the brambles assuming a certificate for large directed treewidth is given. Moreover, we discuss algorithmic applications of our results for the Directed Disjoint Paths with Congestion problem, and to half-integral packings of subgraphs with large directed treewidth.
item.dc:creator: Victor A. Campos, Raul Lopes, Rodrigo Nogueira, Ignasi Sau

item.title: Deterministic Girth Approximation in Weighted Undirected Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.13452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give deterministic algorithms for approximating the girth~$g$ of an undirected graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and nonnegative real edge lengths. For every integer $k\geq2$, our algorithm returns a cycle of length at most $\frac{2k}{3}g$ in $O((m+n^{1+2/k})k\log n)$ worst-case time. For every constant~$k$, this matches the stretch and the expected running time of the randomized algorithms of Kadria, Roditty, Sidford, Vassilevska Williams, and Zwick [SODA'23, SICOMP'26] and Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams [ESA'26]. In general, it loses only a factor of $O(\min\{k,\log n\})$ in the term that depends on~$m$. The best previous deterministic trade-off, of Kadria, Roditty, Sidford, Vassilevska Williams, and Zwick [SODA'22], has stretch~$k$ instead of $\frac{2k}{3}$ at the same exponent (for even~$k$) and requires integer edge lengths. In particular, for $k=3$ we obtain a deterministic $2$-approximation in $O((m+n^{5/3})\log n)$ time for real edge lengths, whereas the deterministic algorithm of Ducoffe [SIDMA'21] for real lengths has stretch $2+\varepsilon$. Our main technical idea is that a deterministic construction of the Thorup--Zwick hierarchy used by these algorithms may stop exploring as soon as it finds a cycle: the approximation analysis only needs clusters truncated at half the best cycle certificate found, so balls stopped in this way need not be hit. Together with a degree-weighted selection rule, this bounds the work of each level by its number of edges and stored ball entries. More generally, a ball need not be hit whenever the analysis only uses clusters up to a radius bounded by a certificate that the algorithm has already found.
item.dc:creator: Avi Kadria

item.title: Breaking Two Barriers for Dynamic Planar Reachability
item.description: arXiv:2610.13473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the reachability problem in fully dynamic directed planar graphs: the graph undergoes edge updates (insertions and deletions) and we receive queries asking if one vertex is reachable from another. The current-best online algorithm for dynamic planar reachability spends worst-case time $\widetilde{{O}}(n^{2/3})$ per query/update [Subramanian, ESA '93]. This can be improved to $\widetilde{{O}}(n^{1/2})$ in the offline setting or when the embedding is fixed [Diks and Sankowski, ESA '07]. Our contribution is twofold: 1. We present the first algorithm that breaks the square-root barrier for dynamic planar reachability in the offline setting, obtaining time ${O}(n^{0.49})$ per query/update. This shows that the problem is easier than answering distance queries in a dynamic undirected planar graph, for which a conditional lower bound of $n^{1/2 - o(1)}$ is known [Abboud and Dahlgaard, FOCS '16]. Notably, this lower bound applies to both online and offline algorithms. 2. Second, in the general online setting we design a randomized data structure with amortized update and query time ${O}(n^{0.664})$. This is the first improvement upon the exponent $2/3$ in over three decades. The main engine behind our theorems is a new sparsification framework aimed at maintaining information about reachability. Specifically, we study digraphs through the lens of VC dimensionality of certain set systems. First, we design sparse reachability emulators for planar digraphs that preserve the VC dimension. Second, we utilize orderings with a low ``stabbing number'' [Chazelle and Welzl, Discrete Comput. Geom. '89] to compute subquadratic reachability emulators in subquadratic time whenever the VC dimension is bounded.
item.dc:creator: Adam Karczmarz, Micha{\l} W{\l}odarczyk

item.title: Tight asymptotic competitive ratio for the Canadian Traveller Problem on unit-weighted grids
item.description: arXiv:2610.13712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the $k$-Canadian Traveller Problem (k-ctp), an online navigation problem introduced by Papadimitriou and Yannakakis in 1991. Given an undirected weighted graph $G=(V,E,\omega)$ and two vertices $s,t\in V$, a traveller aims at navigating from $s$ to $t$ while minimizing the total distance travelled. However, up to $k$ edges of the graph may be blocked, and the traveller discovers that an edge is blocked only upon reaching one of its endpoints. The performance of an online algorithm for k-ctp is measured with the competitive ratio, which is the quotient between the distance actually traversed and the distance traversed by an omniscient traveller who knows all blockages in advance. A general lower bound $2k+1$ for the competitive ratio of deterministic algorithms remains valid even when the input graph is series-parallel, whereas constant competitive ratios can be achieved on restricted graph classes, such as cycles or unit-weighted outerplanar graphs. In this paper, we establish the first intermediate competitive ratio between constant and linear regimes. We prove that, on unit-weighted solid grid graphs, there exists an online algorithm with competitive ratio $O(\sqrt{k})$. This ratio is asymptotically tight and cannot be defeated, even on unit-weighted square grids. Finally, we show that both the unit-weighted and solidity assumptions are essential: going further with arbitrary edge weights (even on square grids) or non-solid unit-weighted grid structures yields a linear lower bound of $\Omega(k)$.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Berg\'e, Vsevolod Chernyshev, Malory Marin, Alexey Pyrko, Lou Sala\"un

item.title: Constructive Arboricity in Almost-Linear Time for Dense Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.13937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The arboricity of a graph is the minimum number of forests needed to partition its edges. We present a randomized algorithm that computes the exact arboricity of a simple graph and constructs an optimal forest partition in $\min\{n^{2+o(1)},m^{4/3+o(1)}\}$ time both in expectation and with high probability, where $n$ and $m$ denote the numbers of vertices and edges. In particular, it runs in almost-linear time, $O(m^{1+o(1)})$, on dense graphs with $m=\Theta(n^2)$. We also give the first known almost-linear-time algorithm that constructs a partition into at most one more forest than optimal.
item.dc:creator: Iman Gholami, Mohammad T. Hajiaghayi, Mahdi JafariRaviz, Alireza Kaviani, Soheil Mohammadkhani, AmirMohammad Shahrezaei

item.title: A Catalytic Algorithm for Transposing Unknown Qutrit Unitaries with Tight Query Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.12664v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct exact deterministic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary $U\in\mathrm{SU}(3)$ using only forward queries. Three queries prepare a catalyst independently of the input state. Four further queries implement transposition while returning the catalyst unchanged and uncorrelated with the output. Two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries and return the same catalyst. Reusing the catalyst implements $m$ transpositions or inversions with $3+4m$ or $3+8m$ total queries, respectively. More generally, we prove that exact transposition and inversion of an unknown $U\in\mathrm{SU}(d)$, $d\ge2$, require at least $d+1$ and $d^2-1$ processing queries, respectively, in fixed causal order. These processing bounds hold for any program state prepared independently of the input state using finitely many forward queries, even if that state is consumed during processing. Both our catalytic qutrit algorithms attain their respective bounds. Moreover, exact qutrit transposition with four processing queries requires at least three preparation queries, and our construction attains this bound.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Ao Chen

item.title: Improved classical optimization of fermionic Hamiltonians beyond Gaussian states
item.description: arXiv:2610.12844v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm that approximates the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$ of a traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonian $H$ on $n$ modes. The algorithm achieves energy at least $\lambda_{\max}/O(\sqrt n)$ and outputs either a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse state in the Fock basis. This is achieved through a new upper bound on $\lambda_{\max}$ in terms of the maximum energy of a Gaussian state and $\sqrt{2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(H^2)}$.
item.dc:creator: Ojas Parekh

item.title: Simultaneous Competitive and Regret Guarantees for TCP Acknowledgment
item.description: arXiv:2610.13571v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study simultaneous competitive and regret guarantees for TCP acknowledgment. Each acknowledgment serves all pending packets, and the objective is to minimize the total acknowledgment and waiting costs. It is well known that no deterministic online algorithm achieves a competitive ratio better than $2$. Given $k$ randomized online experts and $0<\varepsilon<1$, we construct a randomized online algorithm whose realized total cost is always at most $(2+\varepsilon)$ times the offline optimal cost $\mathrm{OPT}$ and whose expected regret against the expert with the smallest realized cost is $O(\sqrt{\mathrm{OPT}\log(k+1)}+\log(1/\varepsilon))$. The algorithm requires no advance knowledge of the number of packets or $\mathrm{OPT}$. Our algorithm controls switching costs between experts and uses the gap between the permitted competitive bound and its current cost to determine when to learn. We also prove lower bounds showing that, for $k\ge 2$, this regret bound is asymptotically optimal in $\mathrm{OPT}$, $k$, and $\varepsilon$, and that $\varepsilon>0$ is necessary for sublinear regret.
item.dc:creator: Tsubasa Harada, Yasushi Kawase, Hanna Sumita

item.title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2610.13717v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair $k$-means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group-average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is $35.8\times$ faster than retraining for the initialization-only model and remains $2.4\times$ and $1.7\times$ faster with one and two fair-refinement rounds, which improve worst-group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about $1.06\times$), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.
item.dc:creator: Aravind Reddy, Deeraj S K, Mohd Wasif Raza, Saurav Prakash

item.title: Exact Algorithms for Distance to Unique Vertex Cover
item.description: arXiv:2502.05059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Horiyama et al. (AAAI 2024) studied the problem of generating graph instances that possess a unique minimum vertex cover under specific conditions. Their approach involved pre-assigning certain vertices to be part of the solution or excluding them from it. Notably, for the \textsc{Vertex Cover} problem, pre-assigning a vertex is equivalent to removing it from the graph. Horiyama et al.~focused on maintaining the size of the minimum vertex cover after these modifications. In this work, we extend their study by relaxing this constraint: our goal is to ensure a unique minimum vertex cover, even if the removal of a vertex may not incur a decrease on the size of said cover. Surprisingly, our relaxation introduces significant theoretical challenges. We observe that the problem is $\Sigma^2_P$-complete, and remains so even for planar graphs of maximum degree 5. Nevertheless, we provide a linear time algorithm for trees, which is then further leveraged to show that MU-VC is in \textsf{FPT} when parameterized by the combination of treewidth and maximum degree. Finally, we show that MU-VC is in \textsf{XP} when parameterized by clique-width while it is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) if we add the size of the solution as part of the parameter.
item.dc:creator: Foivos Fioravantes, Du\v{s}an Knop, Nikolaos Melissinos, Michal Opler, Manolis Vasilakis

item.title: Checking and producing word attractors
item.description: arXiv:2509.08503v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The article focuses on word (or string) attractors, which are sets of positions related to the text compression efficiency of the underlying word. The article presents two combinatorial algorithms based on Suffix automata or Directed Acyclic Word Graphs. The first algorithm decides in linear time whether a set of positions on the word is an attractor of the word. The second algorithm generates an attractor for a given word in a greedy manner. Although the problem of generating a smallest attractor is NP-hard, {the algorithm is efficient and produces very small attractors and even the smallest ones for several well-known infinite families of words.
item.dc:creator: Marie-Pierre B\'eal, Maxime Crochemore, Giuseppe Romana

item.title: Faster and simpler traversal of 0/1-polytopes
item.description: arXiv:2607.17590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recently, Merino and M\"utze (FOCS'23+SICOMP'24) presented an algorithm for computing a Hamilton path on the skeleton of any 0/1-polytope ${\rm conv}(X)$, where $X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$. The algorithm uses as a black box an algorithm for solving the classical linear optimization problem $\min\{w\cdot x\mid x\in X\}$ for some weight vector $w\in\mathbb{R}^n$. The resulting delay per visited vertex on the Hamilton path is only by a $\log n$ factor larger than the time to solve one instance of the optimization algorithm. In this paper, we make the Hamilton path algorithm simpler and faster. Namely, we obtain an amortized delay that is only by a constant factor larger than the running time of the optimization algorithm, thus removing the $\log n$ factor. As concrete results, this yields improved algorithms for generating bases and independent sets in a matroid, spanning trees, forests, matchings and maximum matchings in a graph, vertex covers, minimum vertex covers, independent sets and maximum independent sets in a bipartite graph, and antichains, maximum antichains and ideals in a poset. All of these listings correspond to Hamilton paths on the corresponding polytopes. Furthermore, we obtain an $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP})$ amortized delay algorithm for the vertex enumeration problem on 0/1-polytopes $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid Ax\leq b\}$, where $A\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^m$, and $t_{\rm LP}$ is the time needed to solve the linear program $\min\{w\cdot x\mid Ax\leq b\}$. This improves upon the $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP} \log n)$ delay algorithm of Merino and M\"utze, and the previous $\mathcal{O}(t_{\rm LP}\,n)$ delay algorithm of Bussieck and L\"ubbecke from 1998.
item.dc:creator: Ji\v{r}\'i Fink, Petr Hlad\'ik, Arturo Merino, Ond\v{r}ej Mi\v{c}ka, Torsten M\"utze

item.title: Breaking the 1/3 Barrier for constrained $\boldsymbol{k}$-Submodular Maximization: A Proportional Top-2 Randomized Framework
item.description: arXiv:2609.15677v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: $k$-submodularity generalizes submodularity by allowing each selected element to be assigned one of $k$ labels. We study the maximization of a non-monotone $k$-submodular function, where $k\ge2$, under matroid and knapsack constraints. We develop a proportional top-2 randomized framework that achieves an approximation ratio of $\sqrt2-1\approx0.4142$ under either constraint, breaking the previous $1/3$ barrier. Once an element is selected, its label is chosen from the two labels with the largest marginal gains, with probabilities proportional to their positive parts. The analysis separates replacement, pure-addition, and residual-deletion losses, and proves a sharp local loss certificate for this rule. We then give a Bellman analysis using the same local certificate. It gives a $1/2$-approximation under a cardinality constraint and strengthens the knapsack guarantee to $1/2$ without changing the algorithm. The $1/2$ guarantees are oracle-optimal for $k=2$ and asymptotically tight as $k\to\infty$. The value-oracle complexities are $O(Bnk)$ for cardinality, where $B$ is the cardinality bound, $O(n^2k)$ for matroid, and $O(n^3k^2)$ for knapsack.
item.dc:creator: Siyuan Chen, Shengminjie Chen, Suixiang Gao, Zheyu Jiang, Chenhao Wang, Wenguo Yang

item.title: Deterministic Linear-Time Modular Subset Sum
item.description: arXiv:2609.30992v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic $O(m)$-time algorithm for exact modular subset sum over every modulus $m$. The input gives distinct residues and their multiplicities. The algorithm reports all reachable residues and answers one target query. It returns a witness when the target is reachable. The algorithm uses $O(m)$ auxiliary words on an arithmetic word-RAM. This improves Pot\k{e}pa's deterministic $O(m\log m\,\alpha(m))$-time bound under the same input convention. The running time matches the cost of explicitly reporting all $m$ reachability bits. We represent reachable residues as runs along cycles of repeated addition. Newly reached residues pay for scans of partial runs. We process prime factors in increasing order so that cycle rebuilding takes linear time. A theorem on subset sums of distinct units limits the number of adaptive boundary batches to $O(m^{3/4})$. Radix sorting their $O(m)$ total keys also takes $O(m)$ time.
item.dc:creator: Phuoc Dinh Le, Kha Le

item.title: The directed temporal exploration problem
item.description: arXiv:2609.34339v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the temporal exploration problem on temporal digraphs. We prove that a lifetime of $O(n^2)$ suffices to guarantee the existence of a temporal exploration on always-unilateral temporal digraphs. We complement this with a $\Omega(n^2)$ lower bound, even in the case where each snapshot has maximum undirected degree 2; for always-strong temporal digraphs, the lower bound still holds even if the maximum undirected degree is 3. This stands in stark contrast with the undirected setting. For the large minimum degree setting, we show that a lifetime of $4n/3 - 1$ is sufficient and necessary for guaranteeing the existence of a temporal exploration on temporal digraphs where each snapshot is semicomplete. For always-strong temporal digraphs where each snapshot has minimum undirected degree at least $n - c - 1$, we prove that a lifetime of $O(cn)$ guarantees the existence of a temporal exploration, and we also prove that this is asymptotically tight. From a computational perspective, our results for temporal semicomplete digraphs also yield a polynomial-time, factor-$4/3$ algorithm for deciding if a temporal semicomplete digraph admits a temporal exploration within the first $\ell$ snapshots. We complement this showing that no polynomial-time, factor-$(4/3 - \epsilon)$ approximation algorithm exists, even if every snapshot is a tournament, unless P$=$NP.
item.dc:creator: Marcelo Garlet Milani, Lucas Picasarri-Arrieta, Chaoliang Tang, Hehui Wu

item.title: Efficient Algorithms for Online Subadditive Combinatorial Allocations
item.description: arXiv:2610.09050v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For the online combinatorial allocation problem with subadditive valuations, Correa and Cristi (STOC 2023) proved the existence of a $6$-competitive online algorithm, improving on the previous best $O(\log\!\log m)$-competitive online algorithm due to D\"utting, Kesselheim, and Lucier (FOCS 2020), where $m$ is the number of items. However, Correa and Cristi's result is existential, and it was left open whether a constant competitive ratio is attainable via an efficient online algorithm that uses a polynomial number of demand oracle queries. In this work, we answer this affirmatively, giving an expected-polynomial-time $(6 + \epsilon)$-competitive online algorithm for any constant $\epsilon > 0$. Our techniques also recover, in the offline setting, the $(2 + \epsilon)$-approximation result of Feige (STOC, 2006). Finally, when the buyers' valuations are drawn from identical distributions, we exploit symmetry to obtain an improved $(60/11+\epsilon)$-competitive algorithm. Starting with the natural configuration LP relaxation for the problem, our main technical contribution is a recursive Bundle Score Generator (BSG) that resolves item conflicts by assigning correlated scores to the items requested by each buyer. Unlike the Random Score Generator whose existence is shown by Correa and Cristi, our BSG is efficiently computable in expected polynomial time. Moreover, it satisfies a stochastic dominance property that is sufficient to recover both Feige's offline result and Correa and Cristi's online result.
item.dc:creator: Calum MacRury, Rian Neogi, Kanstantsin Pashkovich, Sahil Singla, Siddharth M Sundaram, Chaitanya Swamy

item.title: Directed Global Minimum Cut in Almost-Linear Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.10898v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a randomized reduction from global minimum cut in a directed graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ weighted edges to maximum-flow computations on graphs of total size $\widetilde{O}(m)$. For polynomially bounded integral weights, this yields the first almost-linear $m^{1+o(1)}$-time algorithm [vdBCK+23], improving the previous $m^{1+o(1)}\min\{\sqrt{n},n/m^{1/3}\}$ bound [CLN+22]. Previous work reduced finding the minimum cut to constructing a 1-respecting arborescence, a directed spanning tree with exactly one edge crossing a minimum cut [CLN+22]. They then construct such a tree by sampling from a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate arborescence packing, which currently requires superlinear time. Our algorithm sidesteps constructing the packing entirely and relies on a novel iterative arborescence sampling procedure. We show that, after $O(\log n)$ rounds of sampling, our final arborescence 1-respects the minimum cut with constant probability.
item.dc:creator: Henry Fleischmann, Jason Li, Thatchaphol Saranurak, Benyu Wang

item.title: An ETH-based quasipolynomial lower bound for Dualization
item.description: arXiv:2610.11473v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dualizing monotone Boolean functions (or equivalently, enumerating minimal transversals in hypergraphs) is a long-standing problem whose output-polynomial-time solvability remains open. While various special cases have been extensively studied, the state-of-the-art algorithm for the general case, due to Fredman and Khachiyan, runs in quasipolynomial time. This paper presents a subexponential-time reduction from \textsc{3SAT} to the complement of \textsc{Dual}: Given a 3CNF formula with $n$ variables, the reduction constructs hypergraphs $H$ and $L$ of total size $2^{O(n^{2/3}(\log n)^{1/3})}$ such that $L \subseteq Tr(H)$ and the formula is satisfiable if and only if $L\neq Tr(H)$, where $Tr(H)$ is the set of minimal transversals of $H$. As a consequence of this reduction, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), neither \textsc{Dual} nor \textsc{Dualization} admits an algorithm running in $N^{o(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ time, where $N$ is the input size for \textsc{Dual} and the combined input and output size for \textsc{Dualization}. In particular, \textsc{Dualization} cannot be solved in output-polynomial time under ETH.
item.dc:creator: Yasuaki Kobayashi, Kazuhiro Kurita, Kunihiro Wasa

item.title: The Upper Clique Transversal Problem: Hardness and Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2309.14103v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A clique transversal in a graph is a set of vertices intersecting all maximal cliques. The problem of determining the minimum size of a clique transversal has received considerable attention in the literature. In this paper, we initiate the study of the ''upper'' variant of this parameter, the upper clique transversal number, defined as the maximum size of a minimal clique transversal. We investigate this parameter from the algorithmic and complexity points of view, with a focus on various graph classes. We show that the corresponding decision problem is NP-complete in the classes of chordal graphs, chordal bipartite graphs, cubic planar bipartite graphs, and line graphs of bipartite graphs, but solvable in linear time in the classes of split graphs, proper interval graphs, and cographs, and in polynomial time for graphs of bounded cliquewidth. We conclude the paper with a number of open questions.
item.dc:creator: Martin Milani\v{c}, Yushi Uno

item.title: Classical and Quantum Heuristics for the Binary Paint Shop Problem
item.description: arXiv:2509.15294v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Binary Paint Shop Problem (BPSP) is an $\mathsf{APX}$-hard optimisation problem arising in automotive manufacturing: given a sequence of $2n$ cars, comprising $n$ distinct models each appearing twice, the task is to decide which of two colours to paint each car so that the two occurrences of each model are painted differently, while minimising consecutive colour swaps. Performance is measured by the paint swap ratio -- the average number of colour changes per car -- which directly affects production efficiency and cost. Prior work showed that the Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) at depth $p=7$ achieves a ratio of $0.393$, outperforming the then-best-known classical heuristic, Recursive Greedy, with a proven asymptotic expected ratio of $0.4$ [Phys. Rev. A 104, 012403 (2021)]. More recently, the Recursive Star Greedy (RSG) heuristic was proposed with a conjectured expected ratio of $0.361$. Here, we formally reduce BPSP to weighted MaxCut, yielding an exact Ising formulation, and benchmark two state-of-the-art low-depth QAOA variants -- eXpressive QAOA and Recursive QAOA -- at $p=1$ (denoted XQAOA$_1$ and RQAOA$_1$) against four classical BPSP heuristics. Across instances ranging from $2^7$ to $2^{12}$ cars, XQAOA$_1$ achieves an average paint-swap ratio of $0.357$; in our instance-wise benchmarks, it outperforms RQAOA$_1$ on almost all instances and each of the four classical baselines, including RSG, on every instance. Surprisingly, RQAOA$_1$ deteriorates with problem size despite employing provably near-optimal QAOA$_1$ parameters at each recursive step, eventually falling behind RSG at the largest sizes. To our knowledge, this is the first report of size-dependent performance degradation of RQAOA$_1$ at scale. In contrast, XQAOA$_1$ remains stable across all tested sizes, with no evidence of size-dependent degradation.
item.dc:creator: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Ping Koy Lam, Syed M Assad

item.title: Hamiltonian locality testing and certification do not achieve the Heisenberg limit
item.description: arXiv:2610.03205v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We establish lower bounds for Hamiltonian property testing with access to the time-evolution operator but not its inverse. Each experiment may query the time-evolution operator multiple times, and distances between Hamiltonians are measured in the normalized Frobenius norm. In this model, we show that testing whether a Hamiltonian is $k$-local or $\varepsilon$-far from every $k$-local Hamiltonian requires $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Kallaugher and Liang (TQC'25). We also prove that testing whether an unknown Hamiltonian equals a target Hamiltonian or is $\varepsilon$-far from it requires $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Sinha and Tong (2025). These are the first lower bounds for natural problems in Hamiltonian learning and testing that rule out Heisenberg-limited scaling of $1/\varepsilon$. As a third result, we show that amplitude estimation to precision $\varepsilon$ requires $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total time evolution, recovering the result of Tang and Wright (QIP'26) in the continuous-time query model. All three results follow from the hardness of distinguishing the zero Hamiltonian from a suitably chosen ensemble of random Hamiltonians. We establish this hardness by adapting the continuous-time adversary method to forward Hamiltonian evolution.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Escudero Guti\'errez, Junseo Lee, Sebastian Zur

item.title: Explicit Asymptotic Bounds for Sequential Calibration Beyond $T^{2/3}$
item.description: arXiv:2610.07623v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Probability forecasts are calibrated when predicted probabilities match empirical outcome frequencies: among events assigned a probability $p$, we'd hope that the fraction of positive outcomes is close to $p$. We study the problem of sequential forecasting of binary outcomes. The classical $O(T^{2/3})$ bound on expected cumulative $\ell_1$-calibration error established by Foster and Vohra stood for over two decades until Dagan et al. reduced the exponent $2/3$ by an unspecified constant. We establish a new two-phase recursive labeling strategy for the sign-preservation-with-reuse game that yields the bound $O(n^{\alpha}t^\beta)$ for all choices of space and time. We then sharpen the reduction from upper bounds on sign preservation to calibration by modifying the equivalence of Dagan et al. to use only $O(\log T)$ instances of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game. This lets us establish an explicit bound of $O(T^{0.662942288})$, the first explicit exponent below $2/3$ for sequential calibration, by combining both improvements and choosing explicit feasible parameters.
item.dc:creator: Eric Dai, Maxwell Fishelson
